Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. text.text: Background: Ethnic minority doctors and international medical graduates (IMGs) now make up most applicants to UK specialty training.

Earlier work has reported lower recruitment success for some ethnic groups, but evidence that covers recent cycles, every training level, all recruitment stages and disaggregated ethnic groups is limited.

We describe trends in ethnicity and country of primary medical qualification among applicants to UK specialty training between 2021 and 2025, and compare the odds of receiving a training offer between groups.

Methods: Repeated cross-sectional analysis of national specialty recruitment data published by NHS England for 2021-2025, comprising 328,839 applications to entry-level (ST1/CT1) and higher specialty (ST3+) programmes.

Unadjusted odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for receiving an offer were calculated for each programme with at least 500 cumulative offers, comparing broad ethnic groups with White applicants, sub-ethnic groups within broad groups, and EU/EEA and rest-of-world graduates with UK graduates.
Spearman's rank correlation tested whether programmes with more rest-of-world applicants showed larger ethnic differences.
Ethnicity offers for 2023 were excluded because the published 2023 tables duplicate those for 2021.
Results: Applications rose 3.1-fold, from 36,709 in 2021 to 114,557 in 2025, while annual offers stayed between 16,988 and 19,710.
The share of applications from White applicants fell from 34.9% to 16.0%, and the share from doctors qualifying outside the UK and EU rose from 43.9% to 69.4%.

Asian and Black applicants had lower offer odds than White applicants in every programme analysed (9 entry-level and 12 higher programmes), with the largest differences at entry level in Anaesthetics (Black vs White OR 0.027, 95% CI 0.020-0.036) and Emergency Medicine (Asian vs White OR 0.086, 95% CI 0.075-0.098).
Chinese applicants had lower odds in 4 of 9 entry-level and 1 of 12 higher programmes.
Within broad groups, Pakistani and Bangladeshi applicants had lower odds than Indian applicants, and Black Caribbean applicants higher odds than Black African applicants, at both levels.
Rest-of-world graduates had lower odds than UK graduates in all 11 entry-level and 17 higher programmes.
A programme's share of rest-of-world applicants was not significantly correlated with Asian or Black offer ORs (ρ -0.45 to -0.27; all p ≥ 0.22).
Conclusions: Centralised medical recruitment in the UK exhibits some persistent ethnic and international qualification disparities despite rising application diversity.
The findings highlight the necessity of disaggregating ethnic groups and addressing subjective evaluation vulnerabilities within multi-stage recruitment processes to foster equity.
The United Kingdom is ethnically diverse.
In the 2021 Census of England and Wales, 81.7% of the population identified as White, 9.3% as Asian, 4.0% as Black, 2.9% as Mixed and 0.7% as Chinese [1].

text.text: A workforce that reflects the population it serves matters for patients and for the health service.

Diverse teams have been associated with better problem solving, communication and patient outcomes [4], and doctors who can progress according to their ability are more likely to remain in the workforce.

text.text: Yet differences in career progression by ethnicity are well documented.

Doctors from ethnic minority backgrounds have lower attainment in undergraduate and postgraduate assessments [5], describe barriers in training relationships and assessment [6], and are under-represented in senior roles across the NHS [7].

text.text: Entry to specialty training in the UK is through national recruitment processes that are intended to be fair and transparent.

The number of UK medical school places is capped by government and managed by national bodies such as the Office for Students and the Department of Health and Social Care [9, 10], in line with workforce policy such as the NHS Long Term Workforce Plan [11].

text.text: In 2019 the Resident Labour Market Test for medical specialty training was lifted when all medical practitioners were added to the Shortage Occupation List, so that international medical graduates (IMGs) could apply for UK specialty training on equal terms with UK graduates [12].

text.text: Applications from IMGs then rose sharply, competition ratios for many specialties increased [13, 14], and IMGs now form a large part of the medical workforce [15].

text.text: We extend this work using the national recruitment data that NHS England publishes for every specialty and level, adding the 2025 recruitment round, all three recruitment stages (application, offer and acceptance), disaggregated sub-ethnic groups, and country of qualification.

Our aims were to describe trends in self-reported ethnicity and country of qualification among applicants to UK specialty training between 2021 and 2025, to describe how representation varies between specialties and recruitment stages, and to compare the odds of receiving an offer between ethnic groups, between sub-ethnic groups, and between UK graduates and IMGs.
We conducted a repeated cross-sectional analysis of national specialty training recruitment data for the 2021 to 2025 recruitment years.

NHS England publishes, for each recruitment year, tables of applications made, appointable applicants, offers made and offers accepted, broken down by programme and entry level, for self-reported ethnicity and for country of primary medical qualification [21].
text.formatted: NHS England publishes, for each recruitment year, tables of applications made, appointable applicants, offers made and offers accepted, broken down by programme and entry level, for self-reported ethnicity and for country of primary medical qualification <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[21]</ref>.

text.text: These programmes are recruited nationally for posts across the UK.
Ethnicity and country of qualification are reported in separate tables and cannot be linked.
Counts refer to applications, not individual applicants: one doctor applying to several programmes contributes one application to each.
Before analysis we checked the downloaded tables against the NHS England web pages (snapshots saved 10 November 2026).

The 2023 ethnicity tables for offers made and offers accepted published by NHS England are cell-for-cell identical to the 2021 tables, including the 2021 programme list and category labels, whereas the 2023 applications table is specific to 2023.

We therefore excluded 2023 ethnicity offers and acceptances; 2023 ethnicity applications are reported descriptively but, because offer odds are calculated only from programme-years with both applications and offers, 2023 does not contribute to any ethnicity odds ratio.
Programme titles were harmonised across years to account for changes in nomenclature.
Acute Care Common Stem routes were combined with their parent specialty (for example, ACCS Emergency Medicine with Emergency Medicine, and ACCS Internal Medicine with Internal Medicine Training).
Programmes were grouped by entry level into entry-level training (ST1/CT1, including CT1 and ST1/2 entry points) and higher specialty training (ST3 and above).
In total, 61 programmes were represented.
Ethnicity was self-reported using 16 categories plus 'not stated'.

Following the categories in the published data, these were grouped into six broad groups: White (British, Irish, any other White background), Asian (Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, any other Asian background), Black (African, Caribbean, any other Black background), Mixed (White and Asian, White and Black African, White and Black Caribbean, any other mixed background), Chinese, and any other ethnic group.
Chinese applicants are reported as a separate category in the source data and were analysed separately.

Because broad groups can hide differences between their members [22, 23], we also compared sub-ethnic groups within the White, Asian and Black groups, using the largest subgroup as the reference (White British, Indian and Black African, respectively).

text.text: Applications with ethnicity not stated were described but excluded from comparisons.
Country of primary medical qualification was reported as UK, EU/EEA or rest of world; IMGs were defined as EU/EEA plus rest-of-world graduates.
NHS England suppresses counts below five.
Suppressed cells were set to 2.5, the mid-point of the possible range.
To test the effect of this choice, all analyses of offer odds were repeated with suppressed cells set to 0 and to 5.
For each programme, applications and offers were summed across recruitment years, using only programme-years for which both applications and offers were published.

The odds ratio (OR) for receiving an offer was calculated from the resulting two-by-two table as the odds of an offer in the group of interest divided by the odds of an offer in the reference group, with a 95% CI calculated on the log scale (Wald method).
A continuity correction of 0.5 was added to every cell only when a cell was zero.
These are unadjusted ORs: no regression model was fitted and no covariates were included, because the published tables do not cross-tabulate ethnicity with any other characteristic.
White applicants were the reference group for comparisons between broad ethnic groups, and UK graduates for comparisons by country of qualification.
To limit imprecision, programme-level ORs were calculated only for programmes with at least 500 cumulative offers, following our previous work [24]; all programmes were retained in national totals.

text.text: Composition by programme was shown for programmes with at least 500 cumulative applications, offers or acceptances at the relevant stage.
Within-group comparisons were pooled across programmes meeting the 500-offer threshold, separately for entry-level and higher training, by summing offers and applications (crude pooled OR).
Because crude pooling can be confounded by differences in where subgroups apply, we also calculated Mantel-Haenszel ORs stratified by programme.

To explore whether ethnic differences were larger in programmes with more international applicants, we calculated Spearman's rank correlation between each programme's percentage of applications from rest-of-world graduates (2021-2025) and its Asian vs White and Black vs White offer OR, separately for entry-level and higher programmes.
This is a programme-level (ecological) analysis and does not describe individual applicants.
All tests were two-sided with α = 0.05.
We did not adjust for multiple comparisons; results are presented as estimates with confidence intervals and should be read as descriptive.
Analyses were performed in Python 3.12.5 (pandas 2.2.2, NumPy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.14.1, Matplotlib 3.9.2).
The study is reported following the STROBE guidance for cross-sectional studies.
Between 2021 and 2025 there were 328,839 applications, 269,215 to entry-level and 59,624 to higher programmes.
Annual applications rose 3.1-fold, from 36,709 in 2021 to 114,557 in 2025, whereas the annual number of offers changed little (16,988 to 19,710 in the years with valid data; Supplementary Table S1).

text.text: Using national data covering five recruitment years, we found that the number of applications to UK specialty training roughly tripled between 2021 and 2025 while the number of offers stayed almost constant, and that the growth came mainly from doctors who qualified outside the UK and EU and from Asian and Black applicants.

Across every programme with enough offers to analyse, Asian and Black applicants had substantially lower unadjusted odds of receiving an offer than White applicants, and graduates from outside the UK and EU had substantially lower odds than UK graduates.
Results for Chinese applicants were more variable: odds were lower in some entry-level specialties but similar to those of White applicants in most higher specialty programmes.
There were clear differences within broad ethnic groups.
The most important caveat is that ethnicity and country of qualification cannot be separated in the published data.

Graduates from outside the UK and EU made up 69.4% of applications in 2025 and had much lower offer odds than UK graduates, and they are more likely than UK graduates to be from Asian, Black and other ethnic minority groups.

Part, and possibly much, of the difference between broad ethnic groups is therefore likely to reflect country of qualification and the factors that travel with it, such as visa requirements, familiarity with UK portfolios and assessments, and the timing of the expansion in international applications.

The within-group results are consistent with this: applicants from 'other White' backgrounds, a group likely to include many international graduates, had odds of an offer around a quarter of those of White British applicants at entry level, a difference comparable in size to some of the differences between broad ethnic groups.
Our ecological analysis does not settle the question.

Programmes with more rest-of-world applicants tended to have larger ethnic differences, but the correlations were weak to moderate and not statistically significant, and with only 9 entry-level and 12 higher programmes the analysis had little power.
Programme-level associations also cannot be used to infer what happens to individual applicants.

Studies that obtained cross-tabulated data have found that the ethnic difference in specialty recruitment success is reduced, but not removed, when country of graduation is taken into account [17, 18].

text.text: Differences among UK graduates are arguably the clearest signal of barriers within UK training, and disparities among international graduates raise different questions about induction, support and the conditions under which they apply.
Neither can be measured from the data NHS England currently publishes.
We recommend that NHS England publish recruitment outcomes cross-tabulated by ethnicity and country of qualification, with appropriate disclosure control.
The Medical Training (Prioritisation) Act 2026 makes this more pressing.

Prioritising UK graduates will change who is offered posts, and is likely to narrow the apparent differences between broad ethnic groups in future data, because fewer international graduates will reach the offer stage.

It will not, by itself, show whether ethnic minority UK graduates are treated equitably, and without cross-tabulated data a narrowing of the headline gap could be misread as evidence that any ethnic inequity has resolved.

Pakistani and Bangladeshi applicants had lower offer odds than Indian applicants, and Black Caribbean applicants higher odds than Black African applicants, at both training levels and in the largest programmes.
These patterns may partly reflect different proportions of UK graduates within each subgroup, which we cannot measure.

Whatever their cause, they show that broad categories such as ' Asian' or the collective term 'BAME' can conceal important differences, and that analyses and interventions should use the most detailed categories the data allow [22, 23].

text.text: Specialty recruitment combines several stages, including the Multi-Specialty Recruitment Assessment for many specialties, scored self-assessment and portfolio review, and interviews.
Differences can arise at any of them.

Ethnic differences in performance in undergraduate and postgraduate assessments are well documented [5, 6]; interviews and other assessments that rely on judgement may be affected by bias, the composition of panels, and differences in communication style [25]; and access to preparation courses, mentorship and portfolio-building opportunities is unequal.

text.text: The published data do not include scores at each stage, so we cannot say where the differences arise.
Stage-level data, including MSRA scores by ethnicity and country of qualification, would allow this to be examined.

This study uses national data for every specialty and both entry levels across five recruitment years, includes the application, offer and acceptance stages, analyses sub-ethnic groups and country of qualification, and reports the effect of suppressed cells.
We verified the published tables against their source and excluded duplicated data.
There are important limitations.

First, the ORs are unadjusted, and the data do not allow adjustment for country of qualification, gender, age, socioeconomic background, disability, assessment scores or other characteristics; the results describe differences in outcomes and do not establish their causes.
Second, counts are applications rather than applicants, so doctors who apply to several programmes are counted more than once, and the ORs are not independent across programmes.
Third, ethnicity offers and acceptances for 2023 were unusable because NHS England published the 2021 tables for that year, so the ethnicity odds ratios are based on 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025.
Fourth, suppression of small counts required imputation; national results were insensitive to this, but estimates for small groups were less stable.
Fifth, the 500-offer threshold excluded many smaller specialties, including all programmes in some specialties of interest.
Sixth, ethnicity was not stated on 6-8% of applications, and these applications also had lower offer odds than White applicants, so non-response may be associated with outcome.
Seventh, we made many comparisons without adjustment for multiplicity, although most of the differences we highlight are very large.
Finally, the data contain no information about applicants' experiences of recruitment, which qualitative research is needed to understand [6].

text.text: In conclusion, our findings challenge the assumption that centralised medical recruitment in the UK is entirely meritocratic and free from ethnic bias.

While national training pathways offer robust structural protections at initial entry, the persistent disparities observed in speciality-level offer success rates, particularly for Asian and Black candidates and compounded by country of qualification dynamics and international workforce reliance, suggests the recruitment process may benefit reform to improve its processes and remove any unconscious racial bias [17].

text.text: Specialities highlighted in our study as having particularly low proportions of non-White doctors may also benefit from wider approaches to promote inclusivity and encourage a diverse pool of applicants to consider joining their speciality.

text.text: At entry level, the specialties with the highest percentage of applications from UK graduates were Public Health Medicine, Core Surgical Training, and Anaesthetics, and those with the highest percentage from IMGs were Core Psychiatry, Cardiothoracic Surgery, and General Practice and Public Health (Dual CCT).

At higher level, the highest percentages of UK graduates were in Anaesthetics, Palliative Medicine, and Otolaryngology, and the highest percentages of IMGs in Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Paediatrics, and General (Internal) Medicine (Figure 4; offers and acceptances in Supplementary Figure S7 and Supplementary Figure S8).
